inlineContent.text: The table is built for millions of rows and dozens of columns on large
screens (tens of millions with a column source), and for values that change
many times a second.
The GPU draws the rows and default cells, with the system’s text layout
(kerning, ligatures, fallback fonts, truncation):
Scrolling only reads the cells that come into view; the cells already in
view only move, so a fast flick through a wide table stays within a
120 Hz frame.
A changed value is shown in the next frame without redrawing the rest.
Numbers are formatted once per value shown.
A frame is drawn only when something visible changed (values out of view
change nothing on screen), in step with the header and the scrollers.
The header’s titles, the summary values, and the pictures and videos of
media cells are drawn by the table too, over the system’s header material and
Liquid Glass. Pictures are downloaded once, decoded off the main thread at
their displayed size and kept within
A table of 100,000 rows scrolls as smoothly as one of 20, and 11.9 million
rows of a 1 GB file (through a column source) scroll at 120 frames a second
on a MacBook Pro M1 Max. What remains is the
cost of your data source and delegate, which this article helps keep low.
, its data source and its delegate are main-actor types: the
table only ever calls them on the main thread. Update your data on the main
thread too, and reload right away:

code: let campaigns = try await api.campaigns()   // Off the main actor while waiting.
data.campaigns = campaigns                  // Back on the main actor.

When the table is removed from its window, it releases its pools and stops
its timers and background summaries, computed again when it is shown
again. Background sorts, first searches and copies finish: they follow
the rows, and the table shows their result when it is back.
The table holds its data source and delegate weakly and keeps no references
to your records, only the values it was given.
